title: 9 Scandinavian Christmas Decorations That Look EXPENSIVE (Cost $1)

scenes.text: Sweetheart, the most beautiful Christmas house I ever walked into had almost nothing in it. White walls, a little tree, candles in every window, and straw stars hanging from red thread. It belonged to Mrs. Lindqvist, a Swedish widow at our church in Mansfield, in nineteen fifty-eight. I was fourteen, and I stood in her doorway with my mouth open.
scenes.caption: ALMOST NOTHING IN IT

scenes.text: Today people pay a fortune for that Nordic Christmas look in the catalogs. So tonight I'm giving you nine Scandinavian Christmas decorations that look expensive but cost about a dollar each, the way Mrs. Lindqvist made them. And stay with me, because the last one is the Swedish secret that makes a whole house feel warm, and it's not a decoration at all.
scenes.caption: ABOUT A DOLLAR EACH

scenes.text: Mrs. Lindqvist came from a little town in Sweden, where winter nights start at three in the afternoon. She said when it's dark that long, you learn to make light and warmth out of almost nothing. Straw from the barn, wood scraps, red yarn, paper, and candles. Nothing was bought. Everything was made by hand, at the kitchen table, in the long evenings.
scenes.caption: DARK AT THREE O'CLOCK

scenes.text: The rule in her house was simple. White, red, natural wood, and green. That's all. No tinsel, no blinking lights, no plastic. She said too many colors make a room loud, and Christmas should be quiet. My mother came home from her house and took half the decorations off our tree. My father didn't notice for a week.
scenes.caption: CHRISTMAS SHOULD BE QUIET

scenes.text: So here's the color rule, honey, and it's the first thing that makes it look expensive. Pick white and red, with natural wood and real green. Put away everything else for a year. In a minute I'll show you the first decoration, and you can make it tonight from a bag of drinking straws or a few stalks of wheat.
scenes.caption: WHITE, RED, WOOD, GREEN

scenes.text: Number one. Straw stars. In Sweden they use real wheat straw, soaked in warm water so it bends. You can buy a bundle at a craft store for two dollars, or use paper straws. Lay four straws in a cross, like a star with eight points, and tie them in the middle with red thread, weaving it over and under. Snip the ends to a point.
scenes.caption: STRAW STARS

scenes.text: Hang them on the tree, in the windows, or from a branch over the table. They catch the candlelight and glow like gold. Mrs. Lindqvist made fifty every December, and she gave one to every child at church. I still have mine from nineteen fifty-eight. It's a little crooked now, honey, but so am I.
scenes.caption: SO AM I

scenes.text: Number two. The Julbock, the Yule goat. It's an old Scandinavian Christmas figure, a little goat made of straw tied with red ribbon. Long ago, people said the goat brought the presents, before Santa Claus. You can buy them small, or make one from a bundle of straw, bent and tied into a body, legs, a head and two curly horns.
scenes.query: Swedish straw yule goat red ribbon
scenes.caption: THE YULE GOAT

scenes.text: Put a little one under the tree, or a big one by the front door. My grandchildren thought it was the funniest thing they ever saw, a goat at Christmas. Now they won't let me put the tree up without it. One year it went missing, and we found it in the dog's bed. The dog had decided it was his Christmas present.
scenes.caption: THE DOG'S PRESENT

scenes.text: Number three. Woven paper hearts. These come from Denmark. Fold two strips of paper, one red and one white, in half, round the top like a heart, and weave them together, over and under. It makes a little checkered basket shaped like a heart. Children love making them. You can fill them with candy and hang them on the tree.
scenes.query: woven paper heart baskets red white
scenes.caption: WOVEN HEARTS

scenes.text: If this is helping you, honey, tap the like button for me. It helps Grandma more than you know. And here's a tip for the hearts. Use heavy paper, like old greeting cards or construction paper, not thin wrapping paper, so they hold their shape. And make a little handle from a strip of paper. Mrs. Lindqvist filled hers with raisins and nuts, and the children ate them off the tree on Christmas Eve.
scenes.caption: EAT THEM OFF THE TREE

scenes.text: Number four. Felt ornaments. Little red and white felt hearts, stars, birds and animals, stitched around the edges with white thread and stuffed with a little cotton. A sheet of felt costs about fifty cents and makes six ornaments. You don't need to sew well. Big, simple stitches look homemade and charming, which is the whole point.
scenes.caption: FIFTY CENTS A SHEET

scenes.text: And make felt animals, honey. A little reindeer, a mouse, a fox, a bird. Cut two shapes, stitch them together, stuff them. Give them a tiny black bead for an eye. My granddaughter made a whole family of felt mice one winter, with tiny scarves. They live on my bookshelf all year round now, because I can't bear to put them away.
scenes.caption: A FAMILY OF MICE

scenes.text: So far, the color rule, straw stars, the Yule goat, paper hearts, and felt ornaments. Number five is the one that makes your house glow from the street. A candle in every window. In Sweden, they put a little wooden candle arch in the windows, or a single candle. Use battery candles with a warm light, on a timer, so they come on at dusk.
scenes.caption: A CANDLE IN EVERY WINDOW

scenes.text: And Mrs. Lindqvist told me about Saint Lucia's Day, the thirteenth of December. Before dawn, the oldest daughter in the house puts on a white dress with a red sash and a crown of greens and candles, and brings coffee and saffron buns to her parents in bed. Her daughter did it every year in Mansfield. I asked my mother if I could do it. She said, not with real candles on your head, Ruthie.
scenes.query: Saint Lucia white dress candle crown
scenes.caption: SAINT LUCIA'S DAY

scenes.text: Number six. Natural wood. A few slices of birch log as a candle stand. A plain wooden bowl filled with pinecones. A bare branch from the yard, standing in a jar, hung with straw stars and paper hearts. That's a Scandinavian Christmas tree for almost nothing. Mrs. Lindqvist had one in her kitchen every year, and the children were allowed to decorate it.
scenes.caption: A BRANCH TREE

scenes.text: And bring in the real green, sweetheart. A few cut evergreen branches in a pitcher of water on the kitchen table. A sprig of juniper over a picture frame. A small potted spruce or rosemary tree by the door, with one straw star on top. Real green is what makes a Nordic room feel alive instead of empty, and you can get the branches free at the tree lot.
scenes.caption: REAL GREEN

scenes.text: Number seven. Clove oranges. Take an orange, and press whole cloves into the skin in rows or swirls. Tie a red ribbon around it and hang it, or pile them in a bowl. They smell like Christmas for weeks. They dry out slowly and last until spring. A bag of cloves and a few oranges cost about three dollars, and the smell is worth a hundred.
scenes.caption: THEY SMELL LIKE CHRISTMAS

scenes.text: Use a toothpick to poke the holes first, honey, so the cloves go in easy and your thumbs don't get sore. Danny and I made them every year at the kitchen table, and the whole house smelled like a spice shop. My mother hung them in the closets, too, to keep the moths out of the wool coats.
scenes.caption: LIKE A SPICE SHOP

scenes.text: Number eight. A white table. A white tablecloth or a plain white runner, red napkins, a few straw stars scattered down the middle, candles, and some sprigs of evergreen. That's all. A white table looks clean and elegant, and the food looks even better on it. Mrs. Lindqvist served cinnamon buns on a white table, and they looked like a painting.
scenes.caption: LIKE A PAINTING

scenes.text: And put the red and white everywhere in small doses, honey. A red and white checked dish towel in the kitchen. Red mittens hung on a string over the window. A white wool blanket with a red stripe over the back of a chair. A little red wooden horse on the windowsill, the Dala horse. It's the repetition of those two colors, quietly, all over the house, that makes it look like a catalog.
scenes.caption: SMALL DOSES

scenes.text: And now number nine, the Swedish secret I promised you. It's not a decoration at all. It's called mys, or hygge in Denmark. It means coziness. A warm blanket on the sofa. Candles lit at supper, every night of December, not just on holidays. Hot cocoa or spiced cider on the stove. Time sitting together in the soft light, without the television.
scenes.caption: IT'S CALLED COZY

scenes.text: Mrs. Lindqvist said, the decorations are only to make the room ready, Ruthie. The Christmas is the people in it. I've thought about that every December for sixty-eight years. You can have every straw star in Sweden, and if nobody sits down together, it's just a room. Light the candles, and call the family to the table.
scenes.caption: THE PEOPLE IN IT

scenes.text: So one more time. White, red, wood and green, and nothing else. Straw stars. A little Yule goat. Woven paper hearts. Felt ornaments. A candle in every window. Natural wood and a branch tree. Clove oranges. A white table. And the cozy part, every night. That's how Mrs. Lindqvist made the most beautiful house I ever saw, for almost nothing.
scenes.caption: FOR ALMOST NOTHING

scenes.text: Tell me in the comments, sweetheart. Does your family have a tradition from the old country? Swedish, German, Polish, Irish, anything. I'd love to hear it. The whole playlist of Grandma's Christmas tips is right there on your screen, and I'll see you in the next video. Good night, honey. God jul, as Mrs. Lindqvist used to say.
scenes.caption: FROM THE OLD COUNTRY?
